main.title: Kirby's Adventure
main.summary: Kirby's Adventure is a 1993 platform game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES).

cards.heading: The Copy Ability enters Dream Land
cards.text: Kirby's Adventure is a 1993 platform game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). It is the second game in the Kirby series after Kirby's Dream Land (1992) on the Game Boy and the first to include the Copy Ability, which allows the main character Kirby to gain new powers by eating certain enemies. The game centers around Kirby traveling across Dream Land to repair the Star Rod after King Dedede breaks it apart and gives the pieces to his minions.

cards.heading: Kirby in colour
cards.text: Masahiro Sakurai returned as director after serving the same role for Kirby's Dream Land. He conceived the copy ability to add more challenge and replay value after the last game received criticism for its simplicity. Because the NES hardware had greater graphical power than the Game Boy and programmers were skilled with the now antiquated hardware, HAL Laboratory was able to create impressive visuals. Kirby's Adventure is the first game to depict Kirby in color. Sakurai had always planned him to be pink, much to the surprise of other staff.

cards.heading: The original game and its later returns
cards.text: Kirby's Adventure was well received and commended for its tight controls, level variety, and the new copy ability. In retrospect, journalists have ranked it among the best NES games. It was remade in 2002 for the Game Boy Advance with enhanced graphics and multiplayer support, titled Kirby: Nightmare in Dream Land. The original NES version was re-released later via Nintendo's Virtual Console digital distribution services, the Wii compilation disc Kirby's Dream Collection, the NES Classic Edition, the Nintendo Classics service, and with stereoscopic 3D for the 3D Classics product line for the Nintendo 3DS.

main.title: SimCity 2000
main.subtitle: The City That Shows the Cost of Every Choice
main.summary: SimCity 2000 links urban growth to power, water, transport, land value and pollution.

cards.heading: A city of environmental tradeoffs
cards.text: SimCity 2000 is a city-building simulation connecting energy, water, traffic, land value, pollution and growth. A cheap power plant can increase pollution, while a new road changes access and the traffic around it. Developing a district means supplying services as well as laying out space. The city responds as these choices accumulate.

cards.heading: Power has a place and a cost
cards.text: Power plants differ in cost, lifespan, capacity and pollution. The player must decide where to build them, how much supply the growing city needs and when a more expensive alternative becomes worthwhile. Power production occupies land and affects the places around it, tying the energy budget to the map.

cards.heading: Transport connects the districts
cards.text: Roads, highways, rail and public transport change how districts connect. A new route may relieve one bottleneck while growth creates pressure elsewhere. Planning services and development therefore requires watching the movement they generate. Traffic provides feedback on the relationships between different parts of the city.

cards.heading: A model makes its rules visible
cards.text: Indicators, graphs and citizen reactions let players follow changes that are difficult to see in the buildings alone. The simulation can be repeated and adjusted quickly, making it possible to test another layout or spending decision. Its selected rules determine which relationships respond, giving players a model to learn through observation and experiment.

main.title: Mutant League Football
main.subtitle: Football on a dangerous field
main.summary: Mutant League Football is Mutant Productions' sports game, released by Electronic Arts for Genesis in North America in May 1993.

cards.heading: Football on a dangerous field
cards.text: Mutant League Football is Mutant Productions' sports game, released by Electronic Arts for Genesis in North America in May 1993. It adapts the machinery of Madden NFL '93 to teams of monstrous players and fields filled with hazards. Recognisable football plays coexist with skeletons, aliens, land mines and other ways to lose a player permanently. The basic goal still involves moving the ball and scoring, but the match also becomes a struggle to keep enough of the team alive to continue playing at all.

cards.heading: A play with another purpose
cards.text: Players have health, and collisions or environmental hazards can kill them during a match. Losing a member of the team can change a useful play into a dangerous decision, especially on a field with pits or explosives. Special Nasty Audibles let the team introduce additional tricks, including an exploding ball. Those options turn the ordinary preparation before a snap into another opportunity to interfere with the opposition. The sporting structure remains readable, while each field and malicious adjustment creates a new risk around an otherwise familiar movement of the ball.

cards.heading: Winning by surviving
cards.text: A coach can bribe the referee into penalising the opposing team, whose response may involve killing that official and facing a more demanding replacement. A team that loses too many players can forfeit, making elimination another route to victory. Exhibition games and a season mode give the violence a recognisable competition to unfold within, accompanied by Brian Schmidt's music. The joke works through the relationship between the two systems: football provides the rules and expectations, then the monsters, hazards and dirty tricks make following the next play wonderfully unreliable.

main.title: Ranger X
main.subtitle: A machine and its support vehicle
main.summary: Ranger X is GAU Entertainment's action shooter, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 28 May 1993.

cards.heading: A machine and its support vehicle
cards.text: Ranger X is GAU Entertainment's action shooter, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 28 May 1993. The player pilots a heavily armed flying machine through missions presented with side-scrolling action and introductory wireframe views. Each stage sets targets to destroy before the final confrontation can begin. A support motorcycle called Indra accompanies the main machine, giving the battlefield another moving component. The combination makes positioning unusually important: the player is managing a flying weapon and a ground vehicle within the same stretch of terrain.

cards.heading: Managing the flight
cards.text: The jetpack lifts Ranger X into the air, but its rising temperature limits sustained flight. Landing gives it time to cool, turning the ground into a necessary part of movement rather than something to avoid. The pulse rifle provides a dependable attack, while special weapons draw on a separate energy reserve. Their different uses invite the player to choose equipment for the targets ahead. Flight, landing and firing form a cycle in which a useful elevated position must be balanced against the need to recover and move again.

cards.heading: Finding energy in the landscape
cards.text: Bright areas replenish the energy used by special weapons, making illumination part of the stage's practical geography. Indra can move and fire independently, and entering it provides another protective shield. Those systems create several reasons to change position during a mission: a target may require a better angle, a flight may need to cool down, or a weapon may need more energy. The layered backgrounds and mechanical animation make those spaces impressive to watch, but their strongest contribution is giving the player's machinery several interacting ways to survive inside them.

main.title: The Terminator
main.subtitle: Kyle Reese fights back through time
main.summary: The Terminator is Virgin Games' Sega CD action game, released in North America in June 1993.

cards.heading: Kyle Reese fights back through time
cards.text: The Terminator is Virgin Games' Sega CD action game, released in North America in June 1993. Kyle Reese fights through the future before traveling to Los Angeles in 1984 to protect Sarah Connor. The ten-stage adventure combines platforming and shooting with scenes from the film between levels. The opening expands the war against Skynet into a substantial playable section, giving the journey to the past its own sequence of machines, industrial spaces and confrontations before the film's familiar pursuit takes over.

cards.heading: A future expanded into ten stages
cards.text: Kyle can crouch, jump and fire in multiple directions, with unlimited ammunition keeping attention on positioning and the enemies ahead. The first four stages take place in 2029 as he searches for the time machine. The remaining stages follow the mission to protect Sarah from the Terminator. Creative additions provide a broader range of situations than a direct recreation of the film alone could supply. Movement and shooting connect those episodes, while the inter-level footage places the action back within the recognizable story.

cards.heading: A film license with an album-sized sound
cards.text: Tommy Tallarico's recorded soundtrack makes especially strong use of the CD format, combining rock, pop and electronic music with contributions from other musicians. Brad Fiedel's Terminator theme links the score to the film. The production also used QSound. The richer audio gives the side-scrolling action a scale beyond its small figures, while the movie clips demonstrate another common promise of disc-based games. The score became a defining part of this version's identity, connecting a familiar license to the changing sound of console action.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening
main.subtitle: A Zelda adventure for the Game Boy
main.summary: A portable adventure began after work.

cards.heading: An experiment becomes a project
cards.text: Link's Awakening began without an official commission. In Nintendo's later conversation with Satoru Iwata, Takashi Tezuka remembers Kazuaki Morita experimenting with the available Game Boy development kit. Colleagues joined the work after their normal duties, treating it like an after-school club. The monochrome experiment became interesting enough for Tezuka to request formal development. The project then gained another development kit. Before Koholint had become a finished island, its makers had to discover what kind of Zelda they could build on the smaller machine.

cards.heading: A programmer brings his own interest
cards.text: The conversation links the island's fishing diversion to Morita's enthusiasm. Toshihiko Nakago describes a programmer inclined to make fishing games without being asked; Eiji Aonuma identifies Link's Awakening as an early home for that interest within Zelda. This is a small but telling contribution. Koholint contains activities that need not serve as steps towards a dungeon boss. The team's recollections place some of that character in the interests of a particular colleague, alongside the work required to make the larger adventure function.

cards.heading: Two buttons keep changing roles
cards.text: The original manual explains the portable interface through reassignment. Items and weapons can occupy either action button, with the subscreen used to change the pair. Roc's Feather lets Link jump over pits or avoid attacks; the Power Bracelet lets him lift obstacles and pull objects. New equipment therefore changes what the same small controller can do. A gap or heavy stone becomes a reason to reconsider the selected tools, rather than simply another piece of scenery on a map the player has already learned.

cards.heading: Koholint Island in a pocket
cards.text: On June 6, 1993, Link arrived on Game Boy and woke far from Hyrule, on Koholint Island. Nintendo filled its compact rooms with combinable items, eccentric characters and paths that open as Link gains equipment. The monochrome screen and two action buttons shaped how players explored: changing tools repeatedly gave familiar places new possibilities. The island's unusual inhabitants and setting gave the portable adventure an intimate, uncanny tone.

cards.heading: A Game Boy experiment becomes an original adventure
cards.text: Development began as an effort to port the Super Nintendo Entertainment System game A Link to the Past to the Game Boy, developed after-hours by Nintendo staff. It grew into an original project under the direction of Takashi Tezuka, with a story and script created by Yoshiaki Koizumi and Kensuke Tanabe. The majority of the Link to the Past team reassembled for Link's Awakening, and Tezuka wanted the game world to feel like the television series Twin Peaks. After a development period of one and a half years, Link's Awakening was released in Japan in June 1993 and worldwide later in the year.

cards.heading: Assigning items to the two buttons
cards.text:
Link's Awakening uses the same inventory/control system as in Ultima: Runes of Virtue (released two years earlier). The player can assign any item in the inventory to either the button "A" or "B".

Link's Awakening was the first overhead-perspective Zelda game to allow Link to jump; this enables sidescrolling sequences similar to those in the earlier Zelda II: The Adventure of Link. Players can expand their abilities with items, which are discovered in dungeons and through character interactions. Certain items grant access to previously inaccessible areas and are needed to enter and complete dungeons. The player may steal items from the game's shop, but doing so changes the player character's name to "THIEF" for the rest of the game and causes the shopkeeper to knock out the character upon re-entry of the shop.

cards.heading: Trading, seashells and side quests
cards.text: In addition to the main quest, Link's Awakening contains side-missions and diversions. Collectible "secret seashells" are hidden throughout the game; when 20 of these are found, the player can receive a powerful sword that fires energy beams when the player character is at full health, similar to the sword in the original The Legend of Zelda. Link's Awakening is the first Zelda game to include a trading sequence minigame: the player may give a certain item to a character, who in turn gives the player another item to trade with someone else. It is also the first game in the Zelda series in which the A and B buttons may be assigned to different items, which enables more varied puzzles and item combinations. Other series elements originating in Link's Awakening include fishing, and learning special songs on an ocarina; the latter mechanic is central to the next Zelda game released, Ocarina of Time.

main.title: Lufia & the Fortress of Doom
main.subtitle: Neverland · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Lufia & the Fortress of Doom is Neverland's Super Nintendo role-playing game about the possible return of the Sinistrals, four powerful beings defeated in an earlier age. A descendant of the hero Maxim travels with Lufia and later companions to investigate the threat. The opening lets the player experience the old confrontation before the story moves forward, giving the legend a playable presence. Towns, dungeons and turn-based battles then build a new journey around people who have inherited the consequences of that earlier victory.

cards.heading: A victory becomes another generation’s problem
cards.text: Lufia & the Fortress of Doom is Neverland's Super Nintendo role-playing game about the possible return of the Sinistrals, four powerful beings defeated in an earlier age. A descendant of the hero Maxim travels with Lufia and later companions to investigate the threat. The opening lets the player experience the old confrontation before the story moves forward, giving the legend a playable presence. Towns, dungeons and turn-based battles then build a new journey around people who have inherited the consequences of that earlier victory.

cards.heading: Give every action a useful target
cards.text: Random encounters ask the player to choose physical attacks, spells and other actions for the party. An attack aimed at an enemy already defeated by another companion can be wasted rather than automatically redirected. Planning the round therefore includes estimating how much damage each opponent needs and which character is likely to act first. New equipment and experience increase the party's options, but an efficient encounter still depends on assigning those options sensibly. A routine fight can become costly when several companions commit their efforts to the same target unnecessarily.

cards.heading: The cast gives the journey its weight
cards.text: Lufia, Aguro and Jerin accompany the hero through kingdoms whose local concerns sit alongside the renewed danger. Conversations develop those relationships between the dungeon expeditions, while towns provide equipment and a place to record progress. Taito published the original game in Japan and North America in 1993. The later Lufia II returned to the earlier generation introduced here, turning the opening's legendary figures into the centre of another adventure. The first game establishes that connection by making inherited history part of an intimate travelling party's present.

main.title: Day of the Tentacle
main.summary: Day of the Tentacle, also known as Maniac Mansion II: Day of the Tentacle, is a 1993 graphic adventure game developed and published by LucasArts.

cards.heading: Day of the Tentacle
cards.text: Day of the Tentacle, also known as Maniac Mansion II: Day of the Tentacle, is a 1993 graphic adventure game developed and published by LucasArts. It is the sequel to the 1987 game Maniac Mansion. The plot follows Bernard Bernoulli and his friends Hoagie and Laverne as they attempt to stop the evil Purple Tentacle from taking over the world. The player takes control of the trio and solves puzzles while using time travel to explore different periods of history.

cards.heading: Cartoon influences and SCUMM
cards.text: Dave Grossman and Tim Schafer co-led development, their first time in such a role. The pair carried over a limited number of elements from Maniac Mansion and forwent the character selection aspect to simplify development. Inspirations included Chuck Jones cartoons and the history of the United States. Day of the Tentacle was the eighth LucasArts game to use the SCUMM engine.

cards.heading: Floppy disks, CD-ROM and a remaster
cards.text: Day of the Tentacle was released simultaneously on floppy disk and CD-ROM to acclaim and commercial success. Critics focused on its cartoon-style visuals and comedic elements. Day of the Tentacle has featured regularly in lists of the best games, and has been referenced in popular culture. A remastered version was developed by Schafer's current studio, Double Fine Productions, and released in March 2016, for OS X, PlayStation 4, PlayStation Vita, and Windows, with an iOS and Linux port released in July the same year, and then later for Xbox One in October 2020.

main.title: Samurai Shodown
main.subtitle: The distance before the sword falls
main.summary: SNK’s weapon fighter builds its duels around reach, timing and the danger of committing to a powerful strike.

cards.heading: Warriors with weapons
cards.text: Samurai Shodown is SNK’s weapon-based fighting game, first released in Japanese arcades on 7 July 1993. Its warriors meet in a late-eighteenth-century setting, with swords and other distinctive weapons shaping the distance between them. A match can turn on a well-timed heavy blow, giving the pause before an attack real importance. Haohmaru and the other fighters combine recognisable silhouettes with different reaches and movements. The Neo Geo presentation allows the camera to draw back as opponents separate and move closer when they come together again.

cards.heading: Waiting for the opening
cards.text: A long-reaching slash can punish an opponent who steps forward carelessly, but committing to an attack also creates an opportunity if it misses. The players repeatedly move into and out of that dangerous distance, looking for a moment to strike. Strong hits receive extra emphasis through the presentation, while the referee raises a flag to acknowledge who connected. Items thrown into the arena can briefly change the situation, adding another object to notice without removing the central question of when it is safe to close in.

cards.heading: Sound and distance
cards.text: Traditional Japanese instruments, including shakuhachi and shamisen, help give the encounters a sound distinct from the urban fighting games around them. The backgrounds and character designs extend that setting across the journey towards Amakusa. Camera movement keeps both fighters visible while allowing their large forms to fill the screen at close range. These choices support the same kind of duel: enough room to judge the approach, followed by a sudden exchange with considerable weight. The original game established the cast and weapon-focused identity carried into the series’ sequels.

main.title: Super Mario All-Stars
main.summary: Super Mario All-Stars is a 1993 platform game compilation developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Four Mario adventures become a compilation
cards.text: Super Mario All-Stars is a 1993 platform game compilation developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It contains remakes of four Super Mario games released for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) and the Famicom Disk System: Super Mario Bros. (1985), Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels (1986; released as Super Mario Bros. 2 in Japan), Super Mario Bros. 2 (1988), and Super Mario Bros. 3 (1988). As in the original games, players control the Italian plumber Mario and his brother Luigi through themed worlds, collecting power-ups, avoiding obstacles, and finding secrets. The remakes feature updated graphics—including the addition of parallax scrolling—and music, modified game physics, a save feature, and bug fixes.

cards.heading: Remaking the games for Super Nintendo
cards.text: Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development developed the compilation after completing Super Mario Kart (1992), at the suggestion of the Mario creator, Shigeru Miyamoto. No longer restricted by the limitations of the 8-bit NES, Nintendo remade them for the 16-bit SNES. The developers based the updated designs on those from Super Mario World (1990) and strove to retain the feel of the original games. Nintendo released Super Mario All-Stars worldwide in late 1993 and rereleased it in 1994 with Super Mario World included. It was The Lost Levels' first release outside Japan; it was not released on the NES in Western territories because Nintendo deemed it too difficult at the time.

cards.heading: Anniversary rereleases preserve the collection
cards.text: Super Mario All-Stars is one of the best-selling Super Mario games, with 10.55 million copies sold by 2015. Critics considered it one of the best SNES games and praised the updated graphics and music, but criticized its lack of innovation. All-Stars served as a basis for later Super Mario rereleases and was described by Famitsu as a model for video game remakes. It was rereleased twice for the anniversary of Super Mario Bros.: in 2010 (the 25th anniversary) in a special package for the Wii, and in 2020 (the 35th anniversary) for the Nintendo Switch as part of the Nintendo Classics service. The Wii rerelease sold 2.24 million copies by 2011 but received mixed reviews, with criticism for its lack of new games and features.
